label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**4 out of 5 stars: a real improvement for our small parish, with a few honest limits**

I'm the pastor of a Lutheran congregation in Minneapolis. Chancel AV asked for a review, and I'm writing one mainly for other small churches trying to decide whether this camera is worth the money. That was the question we were asking last winter, and the reviews we found were either written by engineers or read like advertisements. I'm not an engineer, so this will be plain.

**What we bought and why.** Since 2020 we had been livestreaming worship with a webcam. It got us through the pandemic, but it was never good. In February 2026 we bought the Lindqvist Optics PT-20 from Chancel AV for $2,140, plus $95 for the wall mount. Our nave is 92 feet long, and the camera sits on the balcony rail at the back. It has 20x optical zoom, shoots 1080p at 60 frames, and puts out both NDI HX and plain HDMI. It runs on PoE, which in practice meant a single cable up to the balcony instead of a tangle. It feeds into OBS on our old office PC and goes out to our YouTube channel, where we usually have 30 to 60 viewers on a Sunday.

**Setup.** We stored nine presets: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide shot, and two for the chancel steps. Our first Sunday the presets had drifted a few degrees by the time I got to the sermon, which was discouraging. Firmware update 2.4 came out in March and fixed it, and we haven't had the problem since. If you buy one, update the firmware before you do anything else.

The manual is thin and badly translated. I would not have gotten far with it alone. Chancel AV's tech support was excellent, though. Marcy walked me through things on the phone with real patience, and that counts for a lot when you're a 61-year-old pastor and not a technician.

**Running it.** Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, runs the camera from the free web app on a tablet. He learned it in one afternoon. If your volunteers are teenagers or retirees rather than AV people, this matters.

The one quirk we work around every week is that the autofocus hunts when someone walks between the camera and the pulpit. Our solution was to lock focus on each preset. Now it's a non-issue, but you should know about it going in.

**Picture quality.** This is where the camera earned its keep. At Easter Vigil in April we sang the first "Christ the Lord Is Risen Today" by candlelight only. The picture got grainy, but it stayed usable, and you could see the people and the candles. The old webcam would have shown nothing but dots. On a normal Sunday the difference is even plainer. Delores, who is 82 and homebound, called to tell me she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. I'll admit that phone call did more to convince me we'd spent the money well than any spec sheet.

**What it didn't fix.** Our sound. I want to be clear about this because I think some congregations expect a new camera to make the whole stream better. Audio is not the camera's job, and the PT-20 did nothing for our sound problem. If people at home are complaining that they can't hear the sermon, a camera won't help. That's a microphone and mixing question, and it's a separate budget line.

**Who should buy it.** I'd buy it again. But I'll be honest: a congregation under 100, or one with a smaller sanctuary than ours, might do fine with something cheaper. A lot of what we're paying for is the zoom reaching across 92 feet and holding up in low light. If your room is small and well lit, you may not need that.

**Summary:** 4 stars. Good picture, especially in low light, easy enough for a teenager to run, and backed by genuinely helpful support. It loses a star for the early preset drift, the jumpy autofocus, and a manual that isn't much help. And remember it's a camera, not a sound system.
